name: St John on Bethnal Green
summary: A Church of England parish church designed by Sir John Soane, at the centre of its parish since 1828; the building is Grade I listed. It also hosts concerts and live music.

music.notes: Concerts and live music in the church.

accessibility.notes: The Church of England's directory lists a ramp, an accessible toilet and large-print material; it does not say where the ramp is.

evidence.quote: St John on Bethnal Green 200 Cambridge Heath Road London E2 9PA
St John on Bethnal Green is a Church of England parish church in the Diocese of London.
St John on Bethnal Green is a Grade 1 listed building of international significance which has been at the centre of the vibrant parish of Bethnal Green since 1828.
It is one of only three churches to be designed by the world-renowned architect, Sir John Soane.

One of the most distinctive features of Sir John Soane’s third Commissioner Church, St John’s, Bethnal Green, London (built 1826-1828), is the tower.
The Commissioner grant for St John’s was only £16,000 (eventually raised to £17,500), but Bethnal Green was a poor parish, so economies were needed.

story.opened: Built 1826 to 1828 as Sir John Soane's third Commissioner church.
story.then: According to the Sir John Soane's Museum, the Commissioners' grant was only £16,000, later raised to £17,500, and with a poor parish economies were needed, and one commentator began his remarks on the tower with the words 'this monstrous excrescence'. The venue's own website says Chris Gollon's Stations of the Cross were commissioned in 2000 and installed in 2009. Damp and structural damage are plain to see in the building; the church is looking to raise £130,000 for a first stage of work to establish what is needed, and aims to have begun restoration by 2028.
story.now: The venue's own website lists an Evensong service for children, led by a primary school choir. The church is open to visitors on the second Saturday of each month, 11am to 2pm, and can be hired for events.
story.vibe: The venue's own website describes a simple white interior with no stained glass, where Gollon's paintings bring in colour.
worth_knowing: Gollon used his own family and friends as models for the main figures in the Stations of the Cross, including two of his children.
The Financial Times's chief visual art critic, Jackie Wullschläger, has written about Gollon's paintings, according to the church's own website.
